outline.chapter_title: Motivation and Overview of Few‑Shot Tabular Learning
outline.description: Introduces the challenges of learning from small labeled tabular datasets and why leveraging external knowledge, especially Large Language Models (LLMs), is promising. Sets the stage for the FeatLLM framework.
subtopics: Why tabular data remain hard for few‑shot learning
Traditional approaches (feature engineering, transfer learning, self‑supervision)
The rise of LLMs as knowledge bases
Limitations of existing LLM‑based tabular methods
High‑level idea of using LLMs as feature engineers

outline.chapter_title: Fundamentals of Large Language Models and In‑Context Learning
outline.description: Provides the background on LLMs needed to understand how they can be prompted to generate useful rules without any parameter updates.
subtopics: Architecture and pre‑training of LLMs
Prompting, few‑shot examples, and chain‑of‑thought prompting
In‑context learning vs. fine‑tuning
APIs and practical constraints (prompt length, inference cost)
Examples of LLM reasoning over structured data

outline.chapter_title: Problem Formulation for Few‑Shot Tabular Classification
outline.description: Formally defines the supervised tabular classification setting, notation for features, labels, and the low‑shot regime used throughout the paper.
subtopics: Notation: dataset 𝒟, feature set F, class set C
k‑shot sampling and assumptions about feature descriptions
Goal: learn a predictor using only k labeled instances
Evaluation metrics (AUC, accuracy) in low‑shot regime

outline.chapter_title: Designing Prompts to Extract Decision Rules
outline.description: Explains the three‑part prompt structure that guides the LLM to infer causal relationships and then produce explicit rule sets for each class.
subtopics: Basic information block: task description, feature names/types, few‑shot examples
Reasoning instruction block: two‑step chain‑of‑thought (knowledge → rule derivation)
Response instruction block: formatting rules for reliable parsing
Fixed number of rules per class and handling of feature types
Prompt engineering tricks (temperature, order randomization)

outline.chapter_title: Parsing Natural‑Language Rules into Binary Features
outline.description: Covers how the textual rules are transformed into executable code and then into binary indicator features for each sample.
subtopics: Challenges of noisy LLM output (symbol vs. word variants)
... Using the LLM itself as a parser – code generation prompt
... Executing generated Python code safely with exec()
... Constructing binary matrix Z_k for class k
... Handling logical operators (AND/OR) in rules

outline.chapter_title: Learning from Rule‑Based Features: Linear Model with Non‑Negative Weights
outline.description: Describes the simple downstream model that assigns importance to each binary rule, trains on the k labeled samples, and produces class probabilities.
subtopics: Formulation of logits as w·z with ReLU projection (non‑negative weights)
Softmax over classes and cross‑entropy loss
Why a linear model is sufficient after rule extraction
... Training details: optimizer, epochs, early stopping

outline.description: Shows how multiple rule extraction runs with randomness create diverse weak learners; bagging reduces prompt size; ensemble improves robustness.
subtopics: "Bagging" of features/instances per trial
"Temperature" sampling to encourage diverse rule sets
... Averaging probabilities across T trials
... Relation to self‑consistency in LLM outputs

outline.description: Presents the complete end‑to‑end pipeline in pseudo‑code form and discusses computational complexity at training and inference time.
subtopics: Step 1: Sample k shots and compose prompt
Step 2: Query LLM → rules per class
Step 3: Parse rules → binary features
Step 4: Fit linear weights on k shots
Step 5: Repeat for T ensembles; bagging details
Step 6: Inference – apply stored binary features + averaged logits

outline.description: Details the 13 benchmark datasets spanning classic UCI tables to recent/synthetic ones, and describes all comparative baselines used in the paper.
subtopics: Dataset characteristics (size, #features, domain)
Baselines: logistic regression, XGBoost, Random Forest, SCARF, STUNT, TabPFN, In‑context Learning, TABLET, TabLLM
Implementation specifics (LLM backbones, hyperparameters)

outline.description: Presents quantitative results showing FeatLLM’s superiority in AUC, its low inference latency compared with other LLM methods, and ablation studies that isolate each component’s contribution.
subtopics: AUC tables & discussion of top performance across datasets
Comparison of inference/training time (GPU vs. API calls)
Ablation: without weight tuning, without ensemble, without descriptions, without reasoning step
Effect of number of shots on each ablation

outline.chapter_title: Analysis of Generated Features and Robustness to Spurious Correlations
outline.description: Investigates the quality of rule‑based features (AUROC per feature), how tuning filters irrelevant rules, and experiments adding unrelated columns to test robustness.
subtopics: Feature usefulness metric before/after weight tuning
Case study on Heart dataset with injected spurious columns
Why FeatLLM resists irrelevant features (knowledge‐first reasoning)
Limitations when noisy columns are semantically similar

outline.description: Guides readers on choosing ensemble size T and number of rules R per class; discusses trade‐offs between prompt length, performance, and overfitting in low‐shot settings.
subtopics: Sensitivity plots for T and R
Guidelines for setting temperature & top‑p
Bagging ratios for high dimensional tables

outline.description: Summarizes strengths of FeatLLM while acknowledging its focus on low‑shot regimes; outlines extensions such as richer feature families beyond binary rules and interpretability enhancements.
